newsitem.title: USA: Dollar surges broadly as mark and yen slump.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges broadly as mark and yen slump.

text.p: The dollar surged against major currencies Monday as the Italian lira moved closer to joining a proposed single European currency and a Japanese official hinted Japan's interest rates will remain at current historic lows.
The lira rallied against the German mark after a weekend meeting formalised the lira's reentry into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism, sending the dollar sharply higher against the mark as well.
The mark slipped from 997 lire toward 990 after European Union officials formally set 990 as the target rate for the semi-fixed ERM range.
"The dollar strengthened on the back of the decline in the mark against the lira," said John McCarthy, foreign exchange manager at ING Barings.
A report showing West German consumer inflation fell in November also hurt the mark by dampening expectations for higher interest rates in Germany, dealers said.
In Tokyo, Bank of Japan executive director Tadayo Honma warned a banking symposium that continued failures of Japanese financial institutions could not be ruled out.

This came less than a week after Japanese officials shuttered troubled Hanwa Bank and suggested Japan's economy was still too weak to allow an increase in the official discount rate from its meagre 0.5 percent level.
Low Japanese and German interest rates enhance the relative value of higher-yielding U.S. assets denominated in dollars.

"The financial backdrop in the U.S. is pretty dollar supportive, while the focus in Japan is on the soft environment highlighted by the banking problem," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.
The dollar ended at 1.5235 marks, up from 1.5070 late Friday, and at 112.63 yen, up from 111.37.
The British pound fell to $1.6685 from $1.6805. The dollar hit a 21-month high at 1.2905 Swiss francs before closing at 1.2880, up from 1.2708 late Friday.
The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3425 from C$1.3409.
Sterling rose early in the session but later lost ground as investors took profits after a strong sterling rally in recent sessions.

Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke denied reports that Britain would seek to informally link the pound to the proposed single European currency, insisting sterling would remain an independent unit.
With Britain set to unveil its 1997-8 budget Tuesday, investors sold pounds to book profits in case the fiscal plan contains news that hurts the currency.
"Clarke's comments calmed everybody down, but obviously people are still very anxious about sterling," said Finstrom.
The Swiss franc slipped on talk that Swiss pension funds are considering broadening their investment portfolios to include more foreign assets, dealers said.
"There was talk of a large investor buying dollars and marks against the Swiss franc," added Stephen Jury, chief foreign exchange dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland in New York.
